note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · OPEN HEAD
tiles.details: Start with real source-verified Triplasiella panicles in panels 0–1, fresh Texas flowering heads in panel 5, mature reddish spikelets in panel 6 and pale fresh branching spikelets in panel 11. Panels 8–9 show the plant among other low vegetation, but the underground rootstock is obscured and neighbors may be different grasses. The stiff bristly head BEHIND panel 1 belongs to another grass; its warning arrow must remain. Open branches are a first clue, not a confirmed ID: verify the tiny mature lemma and true collar under magnification.
tiles.short: Tiny green or reddish spikelets on a very open, delicate panicle; not species-confirming alone
tiles.status: REAL GREEN/DARK PANICLES AND FIELD HABIT NOW PHOTOGRAPHED — TINY LEMMA NOT YET CERTIFIED

tiles.heading: 02 · CHECK NATIVES
tiles.details: Native LOOK-ALIKE photos in panels 2, 3, 4 respectively belong to purpletop (Tridens flavus), Texas tridens (Tridens texanus) and purple lovegrass (Eragrostis spectabilis). Purpletop can have an airy broadly spreading/drooping panicle TOO. Their glumes and mature lemma sizes must be examined as independent different-species specimens. Do not treat any image of them as a photograph of Triplasiella's true lemma or collar.
tiles.short: Purpletop and Texas tridens are also open!
tiles.status: THREE NATIVE LOOK-ALIKE PANELS RETAINED — THEIR ORGANS DO NOT COUNT AS TRIPLASIELLA

tiles.heading: 03 · MICROSCOPE LEMMA
tiles.details: New CC0 panel 10 shows a REAL isolated-looking pale green flowering bract in close focus and panel 11 shows multiple attached green spikelets. HOWEVER the tiny bract has NOT been independently identified as lower glume, upper glume, lemma or palea, so DO NOT label it a 3-veined lemma. The published target diagnostic is a roughly 2–3-mm three-veined lemma with only its central midnerve protruding as a short point. Needed: a mature source-vouchered floret split apart dorsal side up, 1-mm ruler, actual veins and central mucro continuously visible. The historic 1900 illustration is NOT a photo.
tiles.short: Tiny green bract close-up now visible; only a dissected measured 3-veined lemma can confirm species
tiles.status: REAL INDIVIDUAL GREEN FLORAL BRACT PHOTOGRAPHED — LEMMA ID/3 VEINS/MM MUCRO HOLD

tiles.heading: 04 · TRUE COLLAR
tiles.details: Panels 7 and 12 now show ACTUAL exact-species green external sheath, blade junction and a culm node. Panel 12 demonstrates why the pale STEM NODE is not the ligule; the diagnostic free inner membrane is located at the INSIDE blade–sheath junction. The 2015 Texas Hill Country treatment reports a 1–3-mm membranous ligule with lacerate margin; broader sources describe a ciliate membrane. Neither photo opens its free edge face-on with a true 1-mm scale. Obtain a single source-vouchered collar macro before adding ligule arrows or settling that source disagreement.
tiles.short: Real outer leaf–sheath junction and culm node present; true inner 1–3 mm free ligule still missing
tiles.status: TRUE EXTERIOR COLLAR/NODE PHOTOS AVAILABLE — OPEN INNER LIGULE/MILLIMETER SCALE STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 05 · ROOTED PERENNIAL
tiles.details: Source-identified plants growing on Texas soil appear in panels 8–9; panel 7/12 show exterior lower shoot and leaf insertion. They establish live growth context, NOT a connected pulled-up perennial root crown. The 2015 Hill Country vegetative key reports a cespitose plant without stolons or rhizomes, while broader descriptions mention a knotty rhizomatous base; neither claim can be proven or resolved from these photos. Need an entire source-vouchered plant continuously showing flowering shoot, basal shoots, exposed attached roots and any underground lateral stems (IF PRESENT), preferably with a centimeter ruler. Do not identify mixed surrounding grasses as part of the focal plant.
tiles.short: Living basal shoot and habitat photographed; connected underground perennial crown remains unseen
tiles.status: REAL IN-GROUND FIELD HABIT, OUTER SHEATH AVAILABLE — EXPOSED ROOTED CROWN MISSING

tiles.heading: 06 · MATURE FLORET SPLIT
tiles.details: Panels 6, 10 and 11 now give REAL near-view spikelets and one photographed individual green bract. The bract's identity is UNDETERMINED: we still need a mature specimen with physically separated lower and upper glumes, lemma and palea, each against a genuine 1-mm scale, so we can see 3 dorsal lemma veins and whether ONLY the central midnerve projects as a short mucro. Compare at identical scale to native purpletop rather than mistaking an awned look-alike for Triplasiella. The true free 1–3-mm ligule and extracted connected root crown are also open holds. New macro panels deliberately have zero speculative anatomy arrows.
tiles.short: Mature spikelets and a small real bract now photographed; dissected 3-veined lemma still required
tiles.status: FINE ANATOMY HOLD — BRACT VIEW REAL, LEMMA/GLUME PROOF + INNER LIGULE/ROOTS STILL REQUIRED

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: LOVEGRASS TRIDENS (Triplasiella eragrostoides; old Tridens/Triodia names): two REAL source-labelled mature open-panicle pictures help recognition, but purpletop, Texas tridens and purple lovegrass also have spreading heads. In the SECOND photo, the stiff bristly RIGHT-BACKGROUND grass is NOT this species. Confirm one mature true 3-veined lemma (~2–3 mm) with ONLY midnerve prolonged as a short mucro (not three long awns) plus inner membranous lacerate 1–3-mm ligule, and actual rooted plant. Research clue: Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015 list a Hays County Tharp s.n. TEX-LL voucher under Tridens eragrostoides; ORIGINAL specimen has not been inspected, county hold remains PROVISIONAL.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Panels 7 and 12 now show ACTUAL exact-species green external sheath, blade junction and a culm node. Panel 12 demonstrates why the pale STEM NODE is not the ligule; the diagnostic free inner membrane is located at the INSIDE blade–sheath junction. The 2015 Texas Hill Country treatment reports a 1–3-mm membranous ligule with lacerate margin; broader sources describe a ciliate membrane. Neither photo opens its free edge face-on with a true 1-mm scale. Obtain a single source-vouchered collar macro before adding ligule arrows or settling that source disagreement.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: New CC0 panel 10 shows a REAL isolated-looking pale green flowering bract in close focus and panel 11 shows multiple attached green spikelets. HOWEVER the tiny bract has NOT been independently identified as lower glume, upper glume, lemma or palea, so DO NOT label it a 3-veined lemma. The published target diagnostic is a roughly 2–3-mm three-veined lemma with only its central midnerve protruding as a short point. Needed: a mature source-vouchered floret split apart dorsal side up, 1-mm ruler, actual veins and central mucro continuously visible. The historic 1900 illustration is NOT a photo.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: TARGET Triplasiella eragrostoides — fairly broad open panicle, fine distant branches, darkening small spikelets; prior name Tridens eragrostoides. A midnerve that alone extends as a short projection is a useful fine distinction in Flora Neomexicana. NATIVE purpletop Tridens flavus — spreading/drooping OPEN panicle too, often purplish; beware previous overgeneralization that all Tridens are contracted. NATIVE Texas tridens Tridens texanus — arching open panicle, potentially quite similar from several feet away. Measure/inspect mature spikelet and lemma instead of using panicle outline as sole key. NATIVE purple lovegrass Eragrostis spectabilis — airy colored panicle and tuft, often superficially similar; check florets/lemma architecture in a confirmed plant. Triplasiella vs sandgrass Triplasis: the 2016 taxonomic treatment reports MUCH broader target panicles and different palea keels, plus absence of upper-sheath cleistogamous spikelets; those features are not verified in current images.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: Lovegrass tridens source photograph
panels.caption: LOVEGRASS TRIDENS: a fine open, arching and widely spreading lovegrass-like panicle with tiny dispersed spikelets, unlike compact narrow Tridens heads. Confirmation requires a mature 3-veined lemma, glumes and ligule under magnification, not merely a large airy grass panicle. Historical synonym Tridens eragrostoides is NOT another canonical species. Critical unshown anatomic characters still need macro photographs.
panels.creator: Eric Knight
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: COMPARE 2 · NATIVE Texas tridens (*Tridens texanus*) — arching panicle
panels.caption: OTHER species: real Texas tridens original archived photo; two source-verified gross arrows show an arching flowering axis and bare lower branch portion. Texas tridens can also carry an OPEN head. A measured mature floret and nerve-tip morphology—not branch spread alone—are needed before a high-confidence split.
panels.creator: Gaiacoyote
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: COMPARE 3 · NATIVE purple lovegrass (*Eragrostis spectabilis*) — airy flowering branch spread
panels.caption: OTHER species: purple lovegrass, another native with a loose to spreading flowering panicle. Original source arrows show actual panicle branches and basal tuft, not a Triplasiella diagnostic structure. Eragrostis species require their own true mature spikelet/lemma examination.

The outlines and mature color are visible, but do not mistake the finger for a millimeter ruler or invent the species' 3-veined ~2–3-mm lemma and its central mucro from this undissected view.

panels.caption: A live Triplasiella shoot photographed in Bexar County shows a green blade emerging beside an encircling external sheath. The INNER free 1–3-mm membranous, possibly lacerate ligule is NOT pulled open or measured in this image. Do not arrow the exterior sheath rim as the diagnostic ligule.

panels.caption: Source-identified lovegrass tridens growing among a mixed native grass/forb community in Bexar County. The photo shows slender flowering shoots and leafy ground vicinity, but nearby plants may be OTHER species. It does not show attached exposed roots, the perennial crown, or genuine rhizomes; the Texas literature conflicts on rhizomatous bases.

panels.caption: A tiny pale-green flowering bract from a source-verified plant is held against a finger. This is genuine macro photographic evidence of one grass flower scale, NOT enough to say it is the lemma rather than a glume or palea. Fingerprints give approximate context only: three lemma veins, free tip, central mucro and 2–3 mm measurement are still awaiting calibrated dissection.

panels.label: PALE GREEN ATTACHED SPIKELETS — fresh source-confirmed flower unit details
panels.caption: Several fresh pale green compressed target spikelets remain attached along a thin flowering branch, photographed beside fingers in Sheffield. A spikelet is a whole unit of small florets—not a single lemma or glume. Their green edges and overlap are visible, but precise 2–3 mm mature lemma length, three-vein count and central mucro require another close dissection.

photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
